Behavior: The bird sings only a few times per day, each session lasting about 2–3 minutes. This audio captures one of those rare vocalizations. No other individuals were interacting, and there was no visual contact.

At 05:43 AM in mid-August in Antalya, the environment is in the dawn twilight phase, just before the sun breaks the horizon. This specific low-light threshold acts as the biological trigger for birds to begin their morning vocalizations.It is highly probable that the singing bird is an adult male. In the vast majority of songbird species found in this region, the complex and continuous morning songs are performed exclusively by males.The Kaş region is characterized by a Mediterranean climate and ecosystem. The surrounding vegetation likely consists of dense maquis shrubland, olive groves, carob trees, or Calabrian pines (Pinus brutia).Sustained singing at this hour is a classic example of the "dawn chorus." This acoustic behavior is primarily driven by territorial defense (warding off rival males) and mate communication.

This was recorded near Lake Eymir in Ankara, Turkey on 18.02.2018. Habitat was dominated by evergreen trees but there were also some Rosacea species in small seasonal stream beds. The sound was coming from hills with evergreens (black pine and Lebanon cedar). There were also some openings in between evergreen patches which were covered with steppe vegetation. 

I don't know how to process sound recordings properly so I'm posting it as it is which is unfiltered, unprocessed. The sound quality is really bad because of the distance and wind but if you carefully listen from 00:02 to 00:05 (better with headphones on and at full volume), you will hear a bird calling three times. It is almost reminiscent of dunnock's call but this bird's call has three consistent reps and each rep has a consistent length. We heard it call many times and each call had three "chirps". It goes like "chirp chirp chirp". 

I would be really happy if someone can help me ID this recording because we are conducting a biodiversity project at the lake and this species might be a new species for our checklist! Or it could well be a really common bird calling in a really unusual way. Thanks in advance to those who will try to ID this bird.
